entities.summary:
Porphyry (c. 234 – c. 305 CE), born Malchus in Tyre, Roman Phoenicia, was a pivotal Neoplatonic philosopher whose systematic efforts preserved and transmitted the profound teachings of Plotinus. A scholar of immense breadth, Porphyry's intellectual endeavors spanned logic, metaphysics, ethics, and theology, positioning him as a central figure in the intellectual currents of the late Roman Empire, deeply influencing both pagan thought and the burgeoning Christian intellectual tradition.

After initial studies in Athens under Cassius Longinus, Porphyry moved to Rome around 262 CE, where he became a devoted disciple of Plotinus. During his six years with Plotinus, he meticulously recorded his teacher's lectures and debates, laying the groundwork for his most monumental achievement. Following Plotinus's death in 270 CE, Porphyry undertook the arduous task of organizing Plotinus's often unsystematic writings into 54 treatises, arranging them into six *Enneads* (groups of nine), a collection he prefaced with his own invaluable biographical introduction, *On the Life of Plotinus and the Arrangement of his Works*. Beyond this editorial feat, Porphyry authored numerous original works, including the *Isagoge* (an introduction to Aristotle's Categories), *Against the Christians*, *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, and *Philosophy from Oracles*.
